newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-IMPERILLED SACCHI SAYS HE WON'T QUIT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-IMPERILLED SACCHI SAYS HE WON'T QUIT.

text.p: A defiant Arrigo Sacchi dismissed calls to quit on Thursday after a lacklustre 1-0 World Cup qualifying win against Georgia that outraged fans and increased the clamour for his resignation.

The embattled coach needed a police escort from the dressing room on Wednesday night amid jeers from supporters still smarting from Italy's early exit from this summer's European Championship finals in England.
With his future once again in doubt, Sacchi hit back with a staunch defence of his record and a pledge to soldier on as long as the players stayed behind him.
"I don't intend to resign. This has always been an unpopular job. Sometimes you need to know how to take it on the chin but my patience is infinite," Sacchi told reporters in Perugia.
"I believe in this team and the players in it. We have a great relationship. The group is united and as long as I feel in tune with them there will not be any problems," Sacchi said.

Sacchi, whose reported $1 million a year contract is not due to expire until the 1998 World Cup finals in France, faced his second panning in a week after the Perugia game, accompanied throughout the second half by whistles from near empty terraces.
He was already under fire after opening Italy's World Cup campaign with a 3-1 win away to Moldova last Saturday that was so unconvincing it had critics baying for his head.
"Sacchi, Farewell", the Rome newspaper Corriere Dello Sport said in a front page headline on Thursday.

"Last night in Perugia, the last chapter of Sacchi's history as team coach was written...when you play two games like these ones against Georgia and Moldova, then there's no option but to turn over a new leaf," the newspaper said.
Sacchi blamed injuries and the proximity of the two encounters for some of Italy's problems.
"The fact no one can deny is that we have six points," Sacchi said. "In a year, we've lost just one match (to the Czech Republic at Euro 96) and then we were down to 10 men."
The Georgia game was Italy's last full international before a crucial visit next February 12 to England, who lead Italy in European Group two on goal difference.
Italian Olympic Committee chief Mario Pescante called for calm from fans and the media in the run-up to the clash.
"This match is going to be crucial to Italy's chances of qualifying. We need to get there in an atmosphere of calm," Pescante said.
Pressed by reporters, he pointedly refused to say whether Italy should also get there in an "atmosphere of continuity".
The possibility of a new Italian Football Federation president in place by December has prompted speculation that Sacchi's future may be in jeopardy.
The Federation is now headed by a short term commissioner, Raffaele Pagnozzi, following the failure to elect a new chief in August in the wake of the departure of Antonio Matarrese.
Luciano Nizzola, current Italian League President and the man expected to be appointed the next Federation President, was cautious on Sacchi's future.

He backed Pescante's call for calm and said Sacchi would still be coach when Italy play Bosnia in a friendly in Sarajevo next month. Beyond that, he said, it was "impossible to predict how the federation will behave on the Sacchi issue".
